title: The Man with the Twisted Lip
paragraphs: Isa Whitney, brother of the late Elias Whitney, D.D., Principal of the Theological College of St. George’s, was deeply addicted to opium. As I understand it, the habit began with a foolish experiment during his college days. After reading De Quincey’s account of his dreams and sensations, he soaked his tobacco in laudanum, hoping to produce the same effects. He discovered, as so many others have, that the practice is easier to acquire than to abandon. For years he remained a slave to the drug, inspiring both horror and pity in his friends and relations. I can picture him still: his yellow, pasty face, his drooping eyelids and pin-point pupils, his body huddled in a chair—the ruined remains of a noble man.

One night in June 1889, our doorbell rang at about the hour when a man begins to yawn and look at the clock. I straightened up in my chair. My wife lowered her needlework into her lap, with a little expression of disappointment.
“A patient!” she said. “You will have to go out.”
I groaned; I had only just returned after an exhausting day.
We heard the front door open, a few hurried words, then quick footsteps on the linoleum. The door of our room flew open, and a woman in a dark dress and black veil came in.

“Please forgive me for calling so late,” she began. Then, suddenly losing command of herself, she hurried forward, put her arms around my wife’s neck, and sobbed on her shoulder. “Oh, I’m in such trouble!” she cried. “I need a little help so badly.”
“Why, it is Kate Whitney!” my wife said, lifting her veil. “How you startled me, Kate! When you came in, I had no idea who you were.”
“I did not know what to do, so I came directly to you.” It was always like that. People in distress came to my wife as birds come to a lighthouse.
“It was very kind of you to come. Now have some wine and water, sit comfortably here, and tell us everything. Or would you prefer me to send James off to bed?”
“Oh, no, no! I need the doctor’s advice and help as well. It is about Isa. He has not come home for two days. I am so afraid for him!”

She had spoken to us before about her husband’s troubles—to me as a doctor, and to my wife as an old friend from school. We did our best to soothe and comfort her. Did she know where he was? Could we perhaps bring him home to her?

Apparently we could. She had reliable information that lately, when the craving seized him, he had been visiting an opium den at the far eastern end of the City. Until now, these bouts had lasted only a day, and he had returned in the evening, twitching and exhausted. This time, however, the spell had held him for forty-eight hours. No doubt he was lying there among the dregs of the docks, inhaling the poison or sleeping off its effects. She was certain we would find him at the Bar of Gold in Upper Swandam Lane. But what could she do? How could a young, timid woman enter such a place and drag her husband away from the ruffians surrounding him?

That was the situation, and naturally there was only one answer. Could I not accompany her there? Then another thought occurred to me: why should she go at all? As Isa Whitney’s medical adviser, I had some influence over him and could manage better alone. I gave her my word that, if he really was at the address she had supplied, I would send him home in a cab within two hours. Ten minutes later I had left my armchair and cheerful sitting-room behind and was travelling east in a hansom. It seemed a strange errand at the time, though only what followed could reveal how strange it would become.

The first stage of my adventure, however, presented little difficulty. Upper Swandam Lane is a filthy alley hidden behind the high wharves on the north bank of the river, east of London Bridge. Between a cheap clothing shop and a gin-shop, a steep staircase descended to a dark opening like the mouth of a cave. There I found the den I wanted. I told the cabman to wait and went down the steps, their centres worn hollow by the endless tread of drunken feet. By a flickering oil lamp above the door, I located the latch and entered a long, low room. Brown opium smoke hung thick and heavy in it, and rows of wooden sleeping berths rose in tiers like those in the forecastle of an emigrant ship.

In the gloom I could just make out bodies sprawled in bizarre positions: hunched shoulders, drawn-up knees, heads tilted back, chins pointing upwards. Here and there a dark, dull eye turned towards the newcomer. Small red circles glimmered from the black shadows, brightening and fading as the poisonous substance burned in the bowls of metal pipes. Most of the occupants were silent. Some muttered to themselves; others conversed in strange, low, monotonous tones, their talk spilling out in bursts before suddenly falling silent. Each mumbled his own thoughts with little attention to his neighbour’s words. At the far end stood a small brazier of burning charcoal. Beside it, on a three-legged wooden stool, sat a tall, thin old man, his jaw resting on his two fists and his elbows on his knees, staring into the fire.
As I came in, a sallow Malay attendant hurried towards me with a pipe and a supply of opium, gesturing towards an empty berth.
“Thank you, but I do not intend to stay,” I said. “A friend of mine is here, Mr. Isa Whitney, and I want to speak to him.”
Someone moved and exclaimed on my right. Peering into the darkness, I saw Whitney staring at me, pale, haggard, and dishevelled.
“My God! It’s Watson,” he said. He was suffering a miserable reaction to the drug, every nerve trembling. “Tell me, Watson, what time is it?”
“Almost eleven.”
“On what day?”
“Friday, the nineteenth of June.”
“Good heavens! I thought it was Wednesday. It is Wednesday. Why do you want to frighten a fellow?” He buried his face in his arms and began sobbing in a high-pitched voice.
“I assure you it is Friday. Your wife has been waiting two days for you. You ought to be ashamed of yourself!”

“I am. But you are mistaken, Watson. I have only been here a few hours—three pipes, four pipes, I cannot remember how many. Still, I will come home with you. I would not frighten Kate, poor little Kate. Give me your hand! Have you brought a cab?”
“Yes, there is one waiting outside.”
“Then I will take it. But I must owe them something. Find out how much, Watson. I feel terribly unwell. I cannot do anything for myself.”

I walked along the narrow aisle between the two rows of sleepers, holding my breath against the drug’s foul, stupefying fumes and looking for the manager. As I passed the tall man beside the brazier, I felt a sudden tug at the skirt of my coat. A quiet voice whispered, “Walk past me, then look back.” I heard the words distinctly. I glanced down. They could only have come from the old man beside me, yet he sat apparently as absorbed as before: thin, deeply wrinkled, and stooping with age. An opium pipe hung between his knees, as though exhaustion had made him let it slip from his fingers. I took two steps and turned. Only the greatest effort kept me from crying out in astonishment. He had turned his back on the room so that only I could see him. His body had filled out, his wrinkles had vanished, and his dull eyes had recovered their fire. There, beside the brazier, grinning at my amazement, sat Sherlock Holmes himself. With a slight movement he beckoned me closer. Then, as he half turned towards the room again, he instantly became a doddering old man with slack lips.
“Holmes!” I whispered. “What on earth brings you to this den?”
“Keep your voice as low as possible,” he replied. “My hearing is excellent. If you would kindly dispose of that drunken friend of yours, I should be very glad of a little conversation with you.”
“There is a cab outside.”

“Then please send him home in it. You can safely leave him to himself: he seems too feeble to get into trouble. I suggest you also give the driver a note for your wife, explaining that you have joined forces with me. Wait outside, and I will meet you in five minutes.”

Refusing Sherlock Holmes was difficult. His requests were always so precise, and delivered with such quiet authority. Still, once Whitney was safely inside the cab, my errand would be practically complete. As for what followed, I could wish for nothing better than to join my friend in one of those extraordinary adventures which formed the ordinary pattern of his life. Within a few minutes I had written my note, settled Whitney’s bill, taken him out to the cab, and watched it carry him away into the darkness. Soon afterwards a decrepit figure emerged from the opium den, and I found myself walking down the street beside Sherlock Holmes. For two streets he shuffled along, back bent and steps uncertain. Then he glanced quickly around, drew himself upright, and burst into hearty laughter.
“I imagine, Watson,” he said, “that you suppose I have added opium smoking to my cocaine injections and all the other little weaknesses on which you have kindly offered your medical opinions.”
“It certainly surprised me to find you there.”
“No more than finding you surprised me.”
“I was looking for a friend.”
“I was looking for an enemy.”
“An enemy of yours?”

“Yes, one of my natural enemies—or perhaps I should say my natural prey. In brief, Watson, I am engaged in a most remarkable investigation. I hoped to discover a clue in these drunkards’ incoherent ramblings, as I have done on previous occasions. Had anyone recognised me in that den, my life would not have been safe for an hour. I have used the place for my own purposes before, and the villainous Lascar who runs it has sworn revenge. At the back of the building, near the corner of Paul’s Wharf, there is a trapdoor that could tell some strange stories about what has passed through it on moonless nights.”
“What! Surely you do not mean bodies?”

“Yes, bodies, Watson. A thousand pounds for every poor soul murdered in that den would make us wealthy men. It is the foulest deathtrap along the whole riverside, and I fear Neville St. Clair has entered it never to come out again. But our carriage ought to be here.” He put his two forefingers between his teeth and gave a shrill whistle. A matching whistle answered from a distance, soon followed by rattling wheels and the clatter of horses’ hooves.
“Now, Watson,” said Holmes, as a tall dog-cart came swiftly through the gloom, its side lanterns casting two golden tunnels of light. “You will come with me, won’t you?”
“If I can be any help.”
“A reliable comrade is always helpful, and someone to record the adventure even more so. My room at The Cedars has two beds.”
“At The Cedars?”
“Yes, Mr. St. Clair’s house. I am staying there while I carry out the investigation.”
“And where is that?”
“Near Lee in Kent. There is a seven-mile drive ahead of us.”
“But I know nothing about this.”

“Naturally. You will hear everything shortly. Climb up here. Very good, John; we shall not need you. Here is half a crown. Expect me tomorrow at about eleven. Give the mare her head. Goodbye for now!”

He flicked the horse with his whip, and we sped through a seemingly endless succession of dark, deserted streets. These gradually widened until we were racing across a broad bridge with stone balustrades, the murky river moving sluggishly below. Beyond it stretched another dreary wilderness of brick and mortar. Only a policeman’s heavy, regular tread or the singing and shouting of some late party of revellers disturbed the silence. Dark clouds drifted slowly across the sky, with a star or two shining faintly through their gaps. Holmes drove without speaking, his head bowed upon his chest, apparently deep in thought. Beside him, I wondered what new investigation could be taxing his abilities so severely, but did not dare interrupt his train of thought. We had travelled several miles and were approaching the outer ring of suburban villas when he stirred, shrugged his shoulders, and lit his pipe, like a man who has decided he is taking the best course.

“You have a splendid talent for silence, Watson,” he said. “It makes you an invaluable companion. On my word, I am grateful to have someone to talk to: my own thoughts are far from pleasant. I was wondering what to say tonight when that dear little woman meets me at her door.”
“You forget that I have heard nothing about it.”

“There is just time to explain the facts before we reach Lee. The case seems absurdly simple, yet somehow I cannot find anything to work from. There is plenty of thread, certainly, but I cannot get hold of an end. Let me set it out clearly and briefly, Watson. Perhaps you will catch a glimmer where I see nothing but darkness.”
“Then go ahead.”

“Some years ago—in May 1884, to be precise—a gentleman named Neville St. Clair arrived at Lee. He appeared to have considerable means. He took a large villa, arranged its grounds very attractively, and generally lived in comfort and style. Gradually he made friends locally. In 1887 he married a local brewer’s daughter, and they now have two children. He had no profession, but held interests in several companies. Usually he went into London in the morning and returned each evening on the 5:14 from Cannon Street. Mr. St. Clair is now thirty-seven. His habits are moderate; he is a good husband, an affectionate father, and popular with everyone who knows him. I should add that, as far as we can establish, his present debts total eighty-eight pounds ten shillings, while he has two hundred and twenty pounds in the Capital and Counties Bank. There is therefore no reason to suppose financial worries have been troubling him.

“Last Monday Neville St. Clair went into town a little earlier than usual. Before leaving, he said he had two important errands and would bring his little boy a box of building bricks. By pure chance, shortly after he left that same Monday, his wife received a telegram. A small but valuable parcel she had been expecting was waiting at the Aberdeen Shipping Company’s offices. If you know your London well, you will know those offices are in Fresno Street, off Upper Swandam Lane, where you found me tonight. Mrs. St. Clair had lunch, went into the City, did some shopping, called at the company’s office, and collected her parcel. At exactly 4:35 she found herself walking along Swandam Lane towards the station. Have you followed all that?”
“That is perfectly clear.”

“You may remember how extremely hot Monday was. Mrs. St. Clair walked slowly, looking around for a cab, since she disliked the neighbourhood. As she went along Swandam Lane, she suddenly heard an exclamation or cry. To her horror, she saw her husband looking down from an open second-floor window, apparently beckoning to her. She could see his face quite clearly and described it as terribly agitated. He waved his hands frantically towards her, then disappeared from the window so abruptly that she thought some irresistible force had pulled him back from behind. Her quick feminine eye noticed one peculiar detail: although he had on a dark coat like the one in which he had left for town, he wore neither a collar nor a necktie.

“Certain that something was wrong, she rushed down the steps, for the building was the very opium den where you found me tonight. She ran through the front room and tried to climb the stairs to the first floor. At their foot, however, she encountered the Lascar scoundrel I mentioned. He forced her back and, with help from a Dane employed there as his assistant, pushed her into the street. Distracted by doubts and fears, she hurried down the lane. By exceptional good fortune, in Fresno Street she met an inspector and several constables on their way to their beats. The inspector and two officers went back with her. Despite the proprietor’s continuing resistance, they reached the room where her husband had last appeared. He was nowhere to be seen. Indeed, the entire floor contained nobody except a hideous crippled wretch who apparently lived there. Both he and the Lascar insisted that no one else had occupied the front room that afternoon. Their denials were so emphatic that the inspector hesitated. He had almost decided Mrs. St. Clair had been mistaken when she cried out, sprang towards a small deal box on the table, and tore off its lid. A shower of children’s bricks fell out. They were the toy her husband had promised to bring home.

“That discovery, together with the cripple’s obvious discomposure, convinced the inspector that something serious had happened. The rooms were searched thoroughly, and everything pointed towards a dreadful crime. The front room was a simply furnished sitting-room leading into a small bedroom that faced the rear of one of the wharves. A narrow strip of ground separates the wharf from the bedroom window. At low tide it is dry; at high tide at least four and a half feet of water cover it. The bedroom has a wide window which opens upwards from the bottom. Examination revealed traces of blood on its sill and several scattered drops on the wooden bedroom floor. Hidden behind a curtain in the sitting-room were all Neville St. Clair’s clothes except his coat. His boots, socks, hat, and watch were all there. None of the clothing showed signs of violence, and no other trace of the man could be found. Apparently he must have gone through the window, since there was no other exit. The sinister bloodstains on the sill offered little hope that he could have saved himself by swimming: the tide was at its highest when the tragedy occurred.

“Now for the villains apparently involved. The Lascar was known to have a thoroughly disreputable past. But according to Mrs. St. Clair he was at the foot of the stairs within seconds of her husband’s appearance at the window, so he could hardly have been anything more than an accomplice. He defended himself by professing complete ignorance. He claimed to know nothing of the activities of his lodger, Hugh Boone, and said he could offer no explanation whatever for the missing gentleman’s clothes being there.

“That disposes of the Lascar manager. Now consider the sinister cripple who lives on the opium den’s second floor, certainly the last person to set eyes on Neville St. Clair. His name is Hugh Boone, and anyone who frequents the City knows his hideous face. He begs professionally, though to evade police regulations he pretends to sell a few wax matches. A little way along Threadneedle Street, on the left, you may have noticed a small recess in the wall. There he sits every day, cross-legged, with his tiny stock of matches in his lap. His appearance is so pitiable that a steady sprinkling of charitable coins falls into the greasy leather cap on the pavement beside him. I have watched him more than once, long before I imagined encountering him professionally, and have been astonished by how much he collects in a short time. His looks are so striking that nobody can pass without noticing him: a mass of orange hair, a pale face marred by a terrible scar which draws the outer edge of his upper lip upwards, a bulldog chin, and piercing dark eyes that contrast oddly with his hair. All these distinguish him from ordinary beggars. So does his wit: he always has an answer ready for the jokes passers-by make at his expense. This, then, is the man we now discover lodging at the opium den, the last man to see the gentleman we are seeking.”
“But he is a cripple!” I said. “What could he have done alone against a man in the prime of life?”

“His disability consists of a limp. In every other respect he looks strong and well fed. Surely your experience as a doctor tells you, Watson, that weakness in one limb is often balanced by unusual strength in the others.”
“Please go on with the story.”

“Mrs. St. Clair fainted when she saw the blood on the window. As her presence could contribute nothing to the investigation, the police took her home in a cab. Inspector Barton, who was in charge, searched the premises very thoroughly, but discovered nothing to explain the mystery. They made one mistake by not arresting Boone immediately. He was allowed a few minutes in which he might have spoken to his friend the Lascar. That error was soon put right: he was arrested and searched, but nothing incriminating was found. There were indeed bloodstains on his right shirtsleeve. He showed them a cut near the nail of his ring finger, however, and said that was where the blood came from. He added that he had been at the window a little earlier, and that the stains there must have come from the same cut. He vehemently denied ever having seen Neville St. Clair, and swore he was as puzzled as the police by the clothes in his room. As for Mrs. St. Clair’s claim to have seen her husband at the window, he said she must be mad or dreaming. Still protesting loudly, he was taken to the police station. The inspector stayed behind, hoping the falling tide would reveal a fresh clue.

“It did, though what appeared on the mud-bank was not quite what they feared. As the water receded, it uncovered Neville St. Clair’s coat, rather than the man himself. What do you suppose they found in its pockets?”
“I cannot think.”

“No, I doubt you would guess. Pennies and half-pennies packed into every pocket: four hundred and twenty-one pennies and two hundred and seventy half-pennies. No wonder the tide had failed to carry it away. A human body would be another matter. A strong eddy runs between the wharf and the house. It seemed quite likely that the heavy coat had stayed while the naked body was sucked out into the river.”
“But you said they found all his other clothes in the room. Would he have been wearing only a coat?”

“No, but one could offer a superficially plausible explanation of the facts. Suppose Boone had pushed Neville St. Clair out through the window. Nobody could have witnessed it. What would he do next? Naturally he would realise at once that he must dispose of the incriminating clothes. He would seize the coat and begin to throw it out, then remember that it would float instead of sinking. Time is short: he has heard the struggle downstairs as the wife tried to get up, and perhaps his Lascar accomplice has already told him that the police are approaching along the street. He cannot waste a moment. He rushes to a hidden store of his earnings from begging and crams all the coins he can grab into the pockets, ensuring that the coat will sink. He throws it out. He would have done the same with the other clothing, but hears footsteps hurrying below and has barely time to shut the window before the police arrive.”
“That certainly seems possible.”

“Then, until something better occurs to us, let us use it as a working hypothesis. As I said, Boone was arrested and taken to the station. Nothing, however, could be found to suggest he had ever been in trouble before. He had been known for years as a professional beggar, but otherwise appeared to lead a quiet, blameless life. That is where matters stand. We are no nearer answering any of our questions: what brought Neville St. Clair to the opium den, what happened to him there, where he is now, and what part Hugh Boone played in his disappearance. I admit that I cannot recall another case which looked so simple at first sight and yet proved so difficult.”

As Sherlock Holmes described this extraordinary chain of events, we sped through London’s outskirts, leaving the last scattered houses behind. Soon we were rattling along between country hedges. Just as he finished, however, we passed through two straggling villages where a few windows still showed glimmers of light.

“These are the outskirts of Lee,” my companion said. “Our short drive has taken us through three English counties: from Middlesex, across a corner of Surrey, and finally into Kent. Do you see the light among those trees? That is The Cedars. Beside that lamp sits a woman whose anxious ears have already, I am almost certain, caught the sound of our horse’s hooves.”
“But why have you not been handling the case from Baker Street?” I asked.

“There are many enquiries that have to be made here. Mrs. St. Clair has very kindly given me the use of two rooms. You can be sure she will welcome my friend and colleague. I dread facing her, Watson, with no news of her husband. Here we are. Whoa, there, whoa!”

We stopped before a large villa in its own grounds. A stable-boy ran out to the horse’s head. I jumped down and followed Holmes along the short, winding gravel drive towards the house. As we approached, the door flew open. A small, fair-haired woman stood there in a light dress of mousseline de soie, with soft pink chiffon at her neck and wrists. The flood of light behind her outlined her figure. One hand rested on the door; the other was half raised in eagerness. Leaning slightly forward, her head thrust towards us, her eyes searching and her lips parted, she was a question made visible.
“Well?” she cried. “Well?” Seeing that there were two of us, she gave a hopeful cry. It turned into a groan as she saw my companion shake his head and shrug his shoulders.
“There is no good news?”
“Nothing.”
“Nothing bad?”
“No.”
“Thank God for that. Come inside, though. You must be exhausted after such a long day.”
“This is my friend, Dr. Watson. He has given me invaluable help on several cases. A fortunate chance has allowed me to bring him here and enlist his assistance in this investigation.”
“I am very glad to meet you,” she said, warmly clasping my hand. “I am sure you will forgive any shortcomings in our hospitality when you consider the sudden blow that has fallen upon us.”

“My dear madam,” I replied, “I am an old soldier, accustomed to rough conditions. Even if I were not, I should see that no apology was necessary. I shall be very happy if I can help either you or my friend here.”

“Now, Mr. Sherlock Holmes,” she said as we entered a brightly lit dining-room, where a cold supper stood ready on the table, “I want to ask you one or two direct questions. Please give me equally direct answers.”
“Of course, madam.”
“Do not spare my feelings. I am neither hysterical nor inclined to faint. I simply want to hear your true, honest opinion.”
“About what, exactly?”
“Deep in your heart, do you believe Neville is still alive?”
The question seemed to embarrass Sherlock Holmes. “Speak frankly!” she insisted. Standing on the rug, she looked searchingly down at him as he leaned back in a wicker chair.
“To be frank, madam, I do not.”
“You believe that he is dead?”
“I do.”
“Was he murdered?”
“I would not say that. Possibly.”
“And what day do you believe he died?”
“It was Monday.”
“Then perhaps, Mr. Holmes, you would kindly explain how I came to receive a letter from him today.”
Sherlock Holmes leaped from his chair as though struck by an electric shock.
“What!” he bellowed.
“Yes, today.” Smiling, she held a small piece of paper up in the air.
“May I look at it?”
“Of course.”

In his eagerness he seized it from her, flattened it on the table, drew the lamp closer, and studied it intently. I rose from my chair and looked over his shoulder. The envelope was made of very coarse paper and bore a Gravesend postmark dated that very day—or rather the previous day, since midnight was now well behind us.
“Rough handwriting,” Holmes murmured. “Surely your husband did not write this, madam?”
“No, but he wrote what is inside.”
“I can also see that the person who addressed the envelope had to ask someone for the address.”
“How do you know that?”

“Look: the ink of the name is deep black, having dried naturally. The rest is greyish, showing that blotting-paper was used. If the whole had been written at once and then blotted, none of it would be so black. The writer put down the name, then paused before adding the address. That can only mean he did not know it. A small detail, certainly, but nothing matters more than small details. Now let us examine the letter. Ah! Something else was enclosed!”
“Yes, a ring. It was his signet-ring.”
“And you are certain this is your husband’s handwriting?”
“One style of his handwriting.”
“One style?”
“The way he writes in a hurry. It is very different from his ordinary hand, but I recognise it well.”

“‘My dearest, do not be afraid. Everything will turn out well. There has been a great mistake, which may take a little time to put right. Wait patiently.—NEVILLE.’ Pencil on a book’s flyleaf, octavo size, without a watermark. Hmm! Posted today at Gravesend by a man with a dirty thumb. Ah! Unless I am badly mistaken, the person who moistened the envelope’s flap had been chewing tobacco. And you have no doubts about this being your husband’s writing, madam?”
“None at all. Neville wrote those words.”
“And someone posted them today at Gravesend. Well, Mrs. St. Clair, things look brighter, though I would not yet say the danger has passed.”
“But surely he must be alive, Mr. Holmes.”
“Unless this is a skilful forgery intended to mislead us. The ring itself proves nothing, after all. Someone may have taken it from him.”
“No, no! It is his writing, his very own!”
“Very well. But he could have written it on Monday, and it was only posted today.”
“That could be so.”
“In that case, much could have happened since.”

“Oh, do not take away my hope, Mr. Holmes. I know he is safe. We are so closely in sympathy that I would know if anything dreadful happened to him. On the last day I saw him, he cut himself in the bedroom. I was in the dining-room, yet I rushed upstairs at once, absolutely certain something had happened. Could I sense so small a thing and still be unaware of his death?”

“I have seen enough to know that a woman’s intuition can be worth more than an analytical thinker’s conclusions. This letter certainly gives you strong evidence to support your belief. But if your husband is alive and able to write to you, why does he stay away?”
“I have no idea. It is inconceivable.”
“Did he say anything on Monday before he left you?”
“No.”
“And seeing him in Swandam Lane came as a surprise?”
“A very great surprise.”
“Was that window open?”
“Yes.”
“So he could have called out to you?”
“He could have.”
“But, as I understand it, his cry contained no words?”
“Yes.”
“You took it as a call for help?”
“Yes. He was waving his hands.”
“It could, though, have been a cry of surprise. The astonishment of seeing you unexpectedly might have made him throw up his hands?”
“That is possible.”
“And you believed someone pulled him back?”
“He vanished so abruptly.”
“Perhaps he jumped back. You saw nobody else in the room, did you?”
“No. But that horrible man admitted he had been there, and the Lascar stood at the bottom of the stairs.”
“Quite. As far as you could tell, your husband was wearing his usual clothes?”
“Except for his collar and tie. I clearly saw his bare throat.”
“Had he ever mentioned Swandam Lane to you?”
“Never.”
“Had you ever seen any indication that he used opium?”
“Never.”
“Thank you, Mrs. St. Clair. Those were the main points on which I needed absolute clarity. Now we should have a little supper and go to bed. Tomorrow may be a very busy day.”

We had been given a large, comfortable room with two beds. Exhausted by the night’s adventures, I was soon under the sheets. Sherlock Holmes, however, could go for days—even a week—without rest when an unsolved problem occupied his mind. He would turn it over, rearrange the facts, and examine it from every angle until he either understood it or satisfied himself that his information was inadequate. I soon realised he was preparing to remain awake all night. He removed his coat and waistcoat, put on a loose blue dressing-gown, and wandered about gathering pillows from his bed and cushions from the sofa and armchairs. He piled these into a kind of Eastern divan and settled on it cross-legged, with an ounce of shag tobacco and a box of matches in front of him. In the lamplight I could see him sitting motionless and silent, an old briar pipe between his lips, his eyes fixed unseeingly on a corner of the ceiling. Blue smoke rose around him, and the light picked out his firm, aquiline features. He was sitting like that when I fell asleep. He was still there when a sudden exclamation woke me and I found summer sunshine pouring into the room. The pipe remained between his lips and smoke still curled upwards. A dense tobacco haze filled the room, but the heap of shag I had seen the night before had entirely disappeared.
“Are you awake, Watson?” he asked.
“Yes.”
“Would you enjoy a morning drive?”
“Certainly.”

“Then get dressed. Nobody is up yet, but I know where the stable-boy sleeps. We can soon have the carriage ready.” He chuckled as he spoke, his eyes sparkling. He seemed quite a different man from the sombre thinker of the night before.
I checked my watch while dressing. No wonder the household was still asleep: it was twenty-five past four. I had scarcely finished when Holmes returned to say that the boy was harnessing the horse.

“I want to test a small theory,” he said, pulling on his boots. “Watson, I believe you are standing before one of the greatest fools in Europe. I deserve to be kicked all the way from here to Charing Cross. Still, I think I have found the key to the mystery.”
“And where might that be?” I asked, smiling.

“In the bathroom,” he replied. Seeing my disbelief, he added, “Yes, I mean it. I have just been there, taken it away, and put it in this Gladstone bag. Come along, my boy. Let us see whether it fits the lock.”

As quietly as we could, we went downstairs and out into the bright morning sun. The horse and carriage stood in the road, with the half-dressed stable-boy waiting at the horse’s head. We climbed in and sped along the London Road. A few country carts were already carrying vegetables into the capital, but the villas on either side were as silent and lifeless as a city in a dream.
“In some ways this has been an unusual case,” Holmes said, flicking the horse into a gallop. “I admit I have been as blind as a mole. But learning wisdom late is better than never learning it.”

As we drove through the streets on the Surrey side, the earliest risers were just beginning to peer sleepily from their windows. We followed Waterloo Bridge Road, crossed the river, hurried up Wellington Street, and turned sharply right into Bow Street. The police knew Sherlock Holmes well, and both constables at the entrance saluted him. One took the horse’s head while the other showed us inside.
“Who is in charge here?” Holmes asked.
“Inspector Bradstreet, sir.”
“Ah, Bradstreet! How are you?” A tall, stout officer in a peaked cap and braided jacket had appeared along the stone-flagged passage. “I would like a private word with you, Bradstreet.”
“Of course, Mr. Holmes. Come into my room.”
The room was small, like an office, with an enormous ledger on the table and a telephone fixed to the wall. The inspector took his seat at the desk.
“How can I help you, Mr. Holmes?”
“I have come about the beggar Boone, who was charged with involvement in the disappearance of Mr. Neville St. Clair of Lee.”
“Yes. He appeared in court and was remanded while enquiries continued.”
“So I understand. Is he here now?”
“Down in the cells.”
“Is he behaving quietly?”
“Oh, he is no trouble. But the fellow is filthy.”
“Filthy, you say?”

“Yes. We can scarcely persuade him to wash his hands, and his face is as black as a tinker’s. Once his case is settled, he will get a proper prison bath. If you saw him, I think you would agree that he needs one.”
“I would very much like to see him.”
“Would you? That is simple enough. Follow me. You can leave your bag here.”
“No, I think I will bring it.”
“Very well. This way, please.” He took us along a passage, unlocked a barred door, and led us down a winding staircase into a whitewashed corridor with doors on both sides.
“His is the third door on the right,” said the inspector. “Here we are!” Quietly he slid back a panel near the top and peered inside.
“He is sleeping,” he said. “You have a clear view of him.”

We both looked through the grating. The prisoner lay facing us in a deep sleep, breathing heavily and slowly. He was of medium height, dressed roughly as his occupation suggested. A coloured shirt showed through a tear in his ragged coat. He was indeed as filthy as the inspector had said, but the dirt covering his face could not hide its repulsive ugliness. A broad, raised old scar crossed it from eye to chin, drawing up one side of the upper lip so that three teeth showed in a permanent snarl. A thick mass of vivid red hair hung low over his forehead and eyes.
“A handsome fellow, isn’t he?” the inspector remarked.

“He certainly wants washing,” said Holmes. “I suspected he might, and took the liberty of bringing the necessary equipment.” As he spoke he opened the Gladstone bag and, to my astonishment, pulled out a very large bath sponge.
“He! He! You are an odd fellow,” the inspector chuckled.
“Now, if you would kindly open that door very quietly, we shall soon give him a much more respectable appearance.”

“Well, I see no reason not to,” the inspector replied. “He is hardly an advertisement for the Bow Street cells, is he?” He put his key in the lock, and we entered as silently as possible. The sleeper half turned, then sank back into deep sleep. Holmes bent over the water jug, soaked his sponge, and scrubbed it vigorously twice across and down the prisoner’s face.
“Allow me to introduce,” he shouted, “Mr. Neville St. Clair of Lee, in the county of Kent.”

I have never witnessed anything like it. Beneath the sponge, the man’s face peeled away like bark from a tree. The crude brown colour vanished! So did the terrible scar across his face and the twisted lip that had formed that repulsive sneer! One tug removed the tangled red hair. Sitting up in bed was a pale man with a sad, refined face, black hair, and smooth skin. He rubbed his eyes and stared around in sleepy confusion. Then, suddenly understanding that he had been exposed, he screamed and flung himself face down into the pillow.
“Great heavens!” exclaimed the inspector. “It really is the missing man. I recognise him from the photograph.”
The prisoner turned back with the reckless air of someone surrendering to his fate. “Very well,” he said. “And what exactly am I charged with?”

“With doing away with Mr. Neville St.—Oh, now, you cannot be charged with that, unless they call it attempted suicide,” the inspector said, grinning. “I have served in the force for twenty-seven years, but this beats everything.”
“If I am Neville St. Clair, then clearly no crime has taken place. It follows that you are holding me unlawfully.”
“No crime, but a very serious mistake,” Holmes replied. “You would have been wiser to take your wife into your confidence.”
“It was not my wife. It was the children,” the prisoner groaned. “God help me, I could not let them be ashamed of their father. My God! To be exposed like this! What can I do?”
Sherlock Holmes took a seat beside him on the couch and kindly patted his shoulder.

“If you leave a court to settle the matter,” he said, “publicity will naturally be almost unavoidable. But if you satisfy the police that there can be no case against you, I see no reason why the details need reach the newspapers. Inspector Bradstreet would, I am sure, take notes of whatever you tell us and pass them to the appropriate authorities. In that way the affair would never have to come before a court.”
“God bless you!” the prisoner cried with deep feeling. “I would have accepted imprisonment, even execution, rather than leave my wretched secret as a stain on my children’s family name.

“You are the first people to hear my story. My father taught school in Chesterfield, and I received an excellent education there. As a young man I travelled, became an actor, and eventually found work as a reporter for a London evening newspaper. One day my editor wanted a series of articles about begging in the capital. I offered to write them. That was the beginning of all my adventures. To gather facts for the articles, I had to try begging for myself. My time on the stage had naturally taught me every trick of make-up; among fellow actors I had been famous for that skill. Now I put it to use. I painted my face and, to look as pitiable as possible, fashioned a convincing scar. With a small strip of flesh-coloured plaster I twisted one side of my lip upwards. Then, wearing a red wig and suitable clothes, I took up a position in the business district, apparently selling matches but really begging. I worked there for seven hours. When I returned home that evening, I was astonished to find I had collected twenty-six shillings and fourpence.

“I wrote the articles and thought little more about it. Some time later, however, I guaranteed a bill for a friend and was served with a writ for twenty-five pounds. I had no idea where to find the money, until a sudden thought struck me. I asked the creditor for two weeks’ grace, requested leave from my employers, and spent it begging in the City in my disguise. Within ten days I had earned the money and paid the debt.

“You can imagine how difficult it was to return to hard work at two pounds a week, knowing I could earn the same in a day simply by painting my face, placing my cap on the pavement, and sitting still. My pride fought the attraction of the money for a long time, but the dollars finally won. I abandoned reporting and spent each day in the corner I had first selected. My dreadful face inspired pity, and my pockets filled with copper coins. Just one man knew the truth: the keeper of a disreputable den in Swandam Lane where I used to lodge. From there I could emerge each morning as a filthy beggar and transform myself each evening into a well-dressed man about town. This man, a Lascar, received generous payment for his rooms, so I knew he would keep my secret.

“Before long I was putting aside substantial sums. I do not suggest that any London beggar could earn seven hundred pounds a year—less than my average receipts. I had unusual advantages: my skill with make-up, and my talent for quick replies. Practice improved the latter until I became a familiar character in the City. Pennies, with silver coins among them, streamed in throughout the day. It was a very poor day when I took less than two pounds.

“My ambitions increased with my wealth. I took a country house and eventually married, while nobody suspected my true occupation. My dear wife knew I did business in the City. She had little idea what that business was.

“Last Monday I had finished work and was changing in my room above the opium den. Looking out of the window, I saw, to my horror and astonishment, my wife in the street, staring directly at me. I cried out in surprise and threw up my arms to hide my face. Then I hurried to the Lascar, who knew my secret, and begged him to stop anyone coming upstairs. I heard her voice below, but knew she could not get up. Quickly I stripped off my clothes, put on my beggar’s outfit, and applied my pigments and wig. Even my wife could not have seen through such a complete disguise. Then I realised they might search the room and discover the clothes that would betray me. I flung the window open. In my haste, I reopened a small cut I had given myself in the bedroom that morning. Next I grabbed my coat, already heavy with the copper coins I had just moved into it from the leather bag in which I kept my takings. I hurled it through the window, and it vanished into the Thames. I would have thrown the other clothes after it, but at that instant constables came rushing upstairs. A few minutes later, rather to my relief, I admit, I found myself arrested as Neville St. Clair’s murderer instead of being recognised as the man himself.

“I do not think there is anything else to explain. I meant to keep up my disguise as long as I could, which is why I preferred not to wash my face. Knowing how anxious my wife would be, I took off my ring and, when no constable was looking, gave it to the Lascar. With it I entrusted a hurried note telling her there was nothing to fear.”
“She received that note only yesterday,” Holmes said.
“Good God! What a dreadful week she must have had!”

“The Lascar has been under police observation,” Inspector Bradstreet explained. “I can readily believe he had difficulty posting a letter without being noticed. Most likely he passed it to a sailor who visited his den, and the man forgot it for several days.”
“That must be the explanation,” Holmes said with an approving nod. “I have no doubt of it. But have you never faced prosecution for begging?”
“Often. But what did a fine matter to me?”
“This must end now, however,” Bradstreet said. “If the police are to keep the affair quiet, Hugh Boone must never appear again.”
“I have sworn that by the most solemn oaths a man can take.”

“Then I think it likely that no further action will be necessary. But if you are caught again, everything must be revealed. Mr. Holmes, we certainly owe you a great deal for clearing this up. I wish I understood how you arrive at your conclusions.”
“I arrived at this one,” my friend replied, “by sitting on five pillows and smoking an ounce of shag. Watson, if we drive to Baker Street, I believe we shall arrive just in time for breakfast.”
